explanations.explanation: Paul shuts that door fast, friend. He asks the question himself, then answers, “Certainly not!” He says it again a verse later: “God did not reject His people, whom He foreknew.” I think Paul saw that question coming from a mile away.

Paul asks, “…did God reject His people?” and the very next words are “Certainly not!” No wiggle room, no “well, let me think about it.” Then he adds, “God did not reject His people, whom He foreknew.” That's a man who knows his answer before he finishes the question.

Paul, who calls himself an apostle at the start of this letter (Romans 1:1), says, “I am an Israelite myself, a descendant of Abraham, from the tribe of Benjamin.” He didn't just say he was an Israelite. He brought the whole family tree with him. If anybody has a right to talk about Israel, it's the man with the paperwork.

Close, friend, but Paul doesn't say Judah. He says he's “…from the tribe of Benjamin.” Judah was one of Israel's twelve tribes too (Genesis 49:8, 28), but the text doesn't put Paul in it. It's an easy swap, like grabbing the wrong cookie tin off the shelf.

Paul doesn't name Levi here. He says, “I am an Israelite myself, a descendant of Abraham, from the tribe of Benjamin.” So Benjamin is the tribe on his family tree. Levi was another of Israel's twelve tribes (Genesis 49:5, 28), but Paul isn't pointing to it.

explanations.answer: He is the only one left
explanations.explanation: That's what Elijah, a prophet of Israel, says to God: “I am the only one left, and they are seeking my life as well…” He has just said that the prophets are killed and the altars are torn down. Then he says he's the only one left. I think that's a lonely thing to say, friend. He's telling it to God, though, and that matters.

Elijah doesn't leave any room for a few, friend. He says, “I am the only one left…” That one hurts a little, because it means he's counting himself as the whole list. I think he felt like the last cookie in the tin.

No servant shows up in what Elijah says. His words are, “I am the only one left, and they are seeking my life as well…” He counts exactly one person, and it's himself. I think that tells you how alone he felt.

explanations.answer: They never bowed to the false god Baal
explanations.explanation: God's reply was, “I have reserved for Myself seven thousand men who have not bowed the knee to Baal.” Baal was a false god (1 Kings 18:21, 39). Elijah said he was the only one left, and God points to seven thousand. Elijah was off on his count, and God did the reserving.

explanations.answer: They hid all of God's true prophets
explanations.explanation: That's a fun story, but it isn't in this reply. God says He reserved these men for Himself, and what marks them is that they “…have not bowed the knee to Baal.” Baal was a false god (1 Kings 18:21, 39). The verse doesn't say a word about hiding prophets.

explanations.answer: They rebuilt all of God's torn altars
explanations.explanation: Nice thought, friend, but the reply doesn't say that. God says, “I have reserved for Myself seven thousand men who have not bowed the knee to Baal.” Baal was a false god (1 Kings 18:21, 39). What stands out about these men is who they did not bow to.

Paul says it plainly: “…at the present time there is a remnant chosen by grace.” A remnant is what's left over, like the seven thousand God reserved in Elijah's day. Same pattern, different time. And notice it's chosen, friend, not just lucky.

Paul doesn't bring up a new prophet here. He says, “…at the present time there is a remnant chosen by grace.” A remnant is what's left, like the seven thousand in Elijah's day. So the match is a group, not one person.

Altars were on Elijah's list of things torn down, so I get the pull. But Paul says, “…at the present time there is a remnant chosen by grace.” The match for the seven thousand is a remnant of people. No altar in this verse.

Paul doesn't split it down the middle, friend. He says, “…if it is by grace, then it is no longer by works.” Then he adds that otherwise “…grace would no longer be grace.” Grace doesn't split the bill with works. It's all one or all the other.

Right, there's no partly in Paul's words. He says the remnant is “…chosen by grace.” and then, “…if it is by grace, then it is no longer by works.” He adds, “Otherwise, grace would no longer be grace.” Grace doesn't take on a co-signer.

That's what Paul says: “What Israel was seeking, it failed to obtain, but the elect did.” So Israel went looking and came back without it. The elect are the ones who did obtain it. Paul has been working toward that contrast for a few verses now.

Paul says the opposite, friend. His words are, “What Israel was seeking, it failed to obtain, but the elect did.” So Israel as a whole came up empty on what it was seeking. The elect are the ones who got it.

Paul says, “What Israel was seeking, it failed to obtain, but the elect did.” The elect are the ones God chose, the same people as the remnant chosen by grace. They got what the rest were seeking. Then Paul says, “The others were hardened…”
Priests are a fair guess, but Paul doesn't mention them here. He says, “…but the elect did.” The elect are the ones chosen, the remnant chosen by grace. Nobody gets a job title in this verse.

Elijah was just in the spotlight, so prophets make sense as a guess. But Paul says, “…but the elect did.” The elect are the ones chosen by grace. This verse isn't about a job. It's about who was chosen.

explanations.answer: Eyes that could not see and ears that could not hear
explanations.explanation: That's the phrase, word for word: “…eyes that could not see, and ears that could not hear, to this very day.” Seeing and hearing are exactly what's missing, friend. Paul says it's “…as it is written…” so he's pointing back to Scripture.

explanations.answer: Eyes that saw only dreams and ears that heard only echoes
explanations.explanation: That's poetic, friend, but it isn't what the verse says. The text says “…eyes that could not see, and ears that could not hear…” Nothing gets seen and nothing gets heard. No dreams, no echoes.

explanations.answer: Eyes that saw too much and ears that heard too much
explanations.explanation: It's the other direction. The verse says “…eyes that could not see, and ears that could not hear, to this very day.” That's not too much, that's nothing getting through. Paul says it's “…as it is written…”
